briefing_top_n.title: The memory shortage is causing a repricing of consumer electronics
briefing_top_n.tldr: A memory shortage, driven by the massive demand for High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) in AI data centers, is causing a repricing of consumer electronics. HBM requires significantly more wafer capacity than traditional DDR or LPDDR memory, and manufacturers are prioritizing its production due to high demand and profit margins. This shift is expected to make consumer electronics, particularly affordable smartphones, more expensive globally.

briefing_top_n.title: Premium: What If...We're In An AI Bubble? (Part 2)
briefing_top_n.publisher: Ed Zitron's Where's Your Ed At
briefing_top_n.tldr: This article argues that the AI industry is in a bubble, driven by a lack of genuine demand beyond a few major players like OpenAI and Anthropic. The author posits that the massive investment in data centers and GPUs, like NVIDIA's Blackwell, is not supported by widespread profitability or sufficient construction, leading to potential debt defaults and hardware write-offs. The piece suggests that the current AI boom relies on a hope that someone else will solve the profitability problem, rather than a solid economic foundation.

briefing_top_n.title: News: OpenAI Had A Negative 122% Non-GAAP Operating Margin In Q1 2026, and ChatGPT Growth Has Stalled
briefing_top_n.publisher: Ed Zitron's Where's Your Ed At
briefing_top_n.tldr: OpenAI reported a non-GAAP operating margin of -122% in Q1 2026, losing $1.22 for every dollar earned, totaling approximately $6.95 billion in losses for the quarter. Despite this, the company is reportedly on track to meet its $30 billion revenue goal for 2026, though maintaining current margins would result in over $36 billion in losses. Furthermore, ChatGPT's user growth has stalled, with a conversion rate of around 6% from free to paying customers.

briefing_top_n.title: The One AI Writing Hack Nobody Talks About.
briefing_top_n.publisher: AI News & Strategy Daily | Nate B Jones
briefing_top_n.tldr: A new AI workflow addresses hallucinations by focusing on "project rooms" or "data rooms" rather than just prompt engineering. This approach involves organizing source materials into a structured workspace before task execution, creating artifacts like source inventories, conflict logs, and missing context lists. This process makes the AI's reasoning inspectable and helps prevent errors, transforming AI from a simple tool into a more capable colleague for complex knowledge work.

briefing_top_n.title: FTC to Require Cox Media Group, Two Other Firms to Pay Nearly $1 Million to Settle Charges They Deceived Customers About “Active Listening” AI-Powered Marketing Service
briefing_top_n.tldr: The FTC has ordered Cox Media Group and two other firms to pay nearly $1 million for deceiving customers about an AI-powered marketing service called "Active Listening." The companies falsely claimed the service used smart devices to listen to real-time conversations for ad targeting. In reality, the service merely resold email lists at a markup and did not use voice data at all. The FTC also noted that tricking users into opting into such invasive data collection through terms of service agreements is not valid consent.

cards.title: Anthropic's "Profitability" Swindle
cards.publisher: Ed Zitron's Where's Your Ed At
cards.tldr: A recent Wall Street Journal report claimed Anthropic is nearing its first profitable quarter, citing significant revenue growth and projected operating profit. However, this analysis suggests the "profitability" is a result of accounting maneuvers, specifically a temporary discount on compute costs from SpaceX for May and June. The author argues that Anthropic's core economics, where costs scale linearly with revenue, have not fundamentally changed, and this reported profit is a deliberate "massaging" of numbers to inflate its valuation during a funding round.

cards.title: Opus 4.7 and OpenAI 5.5 Made Your Prompting Style Obsolete.
cards.publisher: AI News & Strategy Daily | Nate B Jones
cards.tldr: Recent advancements in AI models like Opus 4.7 and OpenAI 5.5 have rendered traditional prompt engineering obsolete, shifting the focus to a more collaborative "question method." These new agents are significantly more powerful, requiring users to interact with them as senior partners rather than junior assistants. The "question method" involves posing thoughtful, directive questions that guide the AI's exploration of complex problems, moving beyond simple task delegation to a partnership in knowledge work.

cards.title: Google's take on openclaw
cards.tldr: Google announced Gemini Omni Flash, a new model family capable of any input/output, with the first iteration editing videos. They also released Gemini 3.5 Flash, a faster but more expensive model with a January 2025 knowledge cutoff. Google's answer to open-source coding agents, Gemini Spark, is "coming soon" and aims to work across Workspace.

cards.title: These 5 Infrastructure Giants Secretly Rule AI
cards.publisher: AI News & Strategy Daily | Nate B Jones
cards.tldr: While model providers like OpenAI get attention, infrastructure giants like Cloudflare, Okta, Snowflake, and Stripe are secretly controlling the deployment and success of AI agents. These companies provide critical control layers for runtime, identity, data governance, and payments, which are essential for agents to operate reliably and securely in production. Understanding and engaging with these infrastructure providers is key for teams looking to ship functional AI agents this year.

cards.title: AI Is Too Expensive
cards.publisher: Ed Zitron's Where's Your Ed At
cards.tldr: AI development is currently economically unviable for most companies involved, with hyperscalers investing trillions in data centers and infrastructure but seeing little to no profitable AI-specific revenue. Microsoft, for example, has spent approximately $100 billion on its OpenAI partnership, yet its AI revenues are a fraction of its capital expenditures. For AI to become profitable, revenues must explode, capital expenditure must cease, GPUs must become margin-positive, and revenue must remain consistent, conditions that are currently unmet.

cards.title: Google Spent a Year Stitching MCP, A2A, AG-UI Together. I/O Today.
cards.publisher: AI News & Strategy Daily | Nate B Jones
cards.tldr: Google is consolidating several agent protocols, including MCP, A2A, and AGUI, into a core stack to simplify AI agent development. MCP standardizes tool access, A2A enables agent-to-agent coordination, and AGUI provides a human control layer for complex workflows. While other protocols like A2UI, AP2, and X42 address specific needs like UI rendering and payments, they are not considered part of the core agent stack. The article emphasizes that understanding these protocols is crucial for shaping positive customer experiences in the evolving agentic economy.

cards.title: Import AI 457: AI stuxnet; cursed Muon optimizer; and positive alignment
cards.tldr: A 20-year-old computer virus called fast16.sys has been analyzed, which selectively targets high-precision calculation software to tamper with results, potentially used in weapons programs. Separately, the Muon optimizer has been found to cause a significant portion of neurons to die during model training, leading researchers to develop Aurora, an optimizer that shows improved performance. Finally, a new position paper introduces "positive alignment," advocating for AI systems that actively support human flourishing rather than solely focusing on safety, proposing a decentralized approach to AI governance.

cards.title: FTC to Require Cox Media Group, Two Other Firms to Pay Nearly $1 Million to Settle Charges They Deceived Customers About “Active Listening” AI-Powered Marketing Service
cards.tldr: The FTC has ordered Cox Media Group and two other firms to pay nearly $1 million for deceiving customers about an AI-powered marketing service called "Active Listening." The companies falsely claimed the service used smart devices to listen to real-time conversations for ad targeting. In reality, the service merely resold email lists at a markup and did not use voice data at all. The FTC also noted that tricking users into opting into such invasive data collection through terms of service agreements is not valid consent.

cards.title: Datasette Agent
cards.tldr: Simon Willison has released Datasette Agent, an extensible AI assistant for Datasette that provides a conversational interface for querying data. It can generate charts using the datasette-agent-charts plugin and integrate with image generation tools via datasette-agent-openai-imagegen. The agent is designed to work with various LLMs, including local models, and is extensible through plugins, with future plans for Datasette Cloud integration and personal AI assistant development.

cards.title: Quoting SpaceX S-1
cards.tldr: SpaceX's S-1 filing reveals that the company is leveraging its compute resources for proprietary AI applications like Grok 5, while also offering capacity to third-party customers. Notably, SpaceX has a cloud services agreement with Anthropic, valued at $1.25 billion per month through May 2029, for access to its COLOSSUS and COLOSSUS II compute infrastructure.

cards.title: How fast is 10 tokens per second really?
cards.tldr: Mike Veerman has created an HTML application that simulates Large Language Model (LLM) token output speeds, ranging from 5 to 800 tokens per second. This tool helps users visualize and understand the practical implications of advertised LLM speeds, such as 30 tokens per second. The application's source code is also available.

cards.title: Google I/O, Gemini Spark, Antigravity
cards.tldr: Google announced Gemini Spark, a personal AI agent that integrates with Google apps, at Google I/O. It runs on Gemini 3.5 Flash and a component called Antigravity, which also powers a new closed-source Antigravity CLI replacing the open-source Gemini CLI. Gemini Spark's security measures include isolated VMs and an Agent Gateway with DLP policies to mitigate risks like prompt injection.

cards.title: LWiAI Podcast #245 - TML-Interaction, Claude For Legal, Sam Altman on Stand
cards.tldr: OpenAI has launched new voice intelligence API features, including GPT Realtime 2, emphasizing latency-reasoning tradeoffs and enhanced guardrails. Thinking Machines previewed a low-latency conversational system with a custom inference stack, showing strong interactivity benchmarks but without public access. Anthropic expanded its vertical offerings with Claude for Legal and increased AWS availability, amidst growing ecosystem tensions between model providers and application companies.

cards.title: Was anything good released at Google I/O 2026?
cards.tldr: Google I/O 2026 introduced the Gemini 3.5 family of models, including Gemini 3.5 Flash, which offers significantly faster performance while maintaining high intelligence for coding and multimodal tasks. The company also enhanced its agentic coding IDE, Anti-gravity, with features like scheduled tasks, projects, and new slash commands, aiming to catch up with competitors. For less technical users, Google AI Studio now integrates with Google Workspace apps for building productivity tools, and new consumer-facing AI features in Gemini include improved image and video generation capabilities.

cards.title: llm-gemini 0.32
cards.tldr: The llm-gemini plugin has been updated to version 0.32, introducing support for the new Gemini 3.5 Flash model. This release also includes notes on Gemini 3.5 Flash and an example of a drawing created with the upgraded plugin.

cards.title: Gemini 3.5 Flash: more expensive, but Google plan to use it for everything
cards.tldr: Google has launched Gemini 3.5 Flash, a new model that is more expensive than its predecessors but is being integrated into many of Google's core products and developer tools. Despite the price increase, which makes it nearly as costly as Gemini 3.1 Pro, Google is making it widely available to consumers and developers. This move, alongside similar pricing strategies from OpenAI and Anthropic, suggests a trend of increasing API costs as companies explore customer price tolerance.

cards.title: The last six months in LLMs in five minutes
cards.tldr: The last six months have seen significant advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs), particularly in coding agents which have become reliable enough for daily use. A notable trend is the "November 2025 inflection point," marked by rapid shifts in the "best" performing models and the emergence of "Claws" or personal AI assistants, exemplified by the rapid rise of OpenClaw. Additionally, open-weight models are becoming increasingly capable, with some now performing competitively on consumer hardware, challenging the dominance of frontier models.

cards.title: Glaucous-winged Gull, Brown Pelican, Snowy Egret, Canada Goose
cards.tldr: While on a final morning walk before heading home from PyCon US, the author spotted a Brown Pelican in the Los Angeles River. The author also observed Glaucous-winged Gulls, Snowy Egrets, and Canada Geese, including some goslings near a swan boat lake.
